issues.legal_issue: A widow’s joint release of her inherited estate to the next female heir and a stranger does not operate as a surrender to the heir followed by a transfer from the heir to the stranger.
material_facts: A widow who had inherited her husband’s estate executed a deed of release in favour of her daughter, the next heir, and the daughter’s husband, who was a stranger to the inheritance.

The deed placed the estate in the joint possession of the daughter and her husband; it did not show that the widow surrendered the whole estate to the daughter alone or that the daughter then transferred an interest to her husband.
The daughter was neither an executant nor an attesting witness to the deed.
After the widow’s death, the ultimate reversioners sued to recover the property from transferees.
issues.conclusion: The deed did not constitute a valid surrender of the widow’s estate to the next heir, and it was not binding on the ultimate reversioners.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, surrender works through the widow’s bona fide and total effacement, which accelerates succession to the husband’s next heir; it is not an ex facie transfer and cannot be made in favour of a stranger. A joint transaction benefiting the next heir and a stranger cannot be recast as a surrender to the heir followed by a transfer from the heir where the deed does not support that construction. The Court applied Vytla Sitanna v. Marivada and Rangasami Goundan v. Nachiappa Goundan; treated Nobokishore v. Harinath as not to be extended beyond its setting; and approved Jagrani v. Gaya, while also referring to Debi Prosad v. Gola Bhagat, Abhay Padha v. Ramkinkar, Yeshwanta v. Antu and Bala Dhondi v. Baya.

rule.if: reversioner_possession_suit and widow_inherited_limited_estate and widow_released_jointly_to_next_heir_and_stranger and not next_heir_received_estate_alone_or_transferred_interest

predicates.reversioner_possession_suit: A claimant who asserts a right as the ultimate successor brings a suit to recover inherited property from transferees.
predicates.widow_inherited_limited_estate: A widow held property as a limited estate inherited from her husband.
predicates.widow_released_jointly_to_next_heir_and_: The widow executed a release placing the estate jointly in the hands of the next heir and a person who was a stranger to the inheritance.
predicates.next_heir_received_estate_alone_or_trans: The next heir received the whole estate alone and then transferred an interest to the stranger.

issues.definition: When an ultimate successor sues to recover property and a widow who held an inherited limited estate released it jointly to the next heir and a stranger, without the next heir first receiving the estate alone or transferring an interest, the joint release does not bind the ultimate successors.

issues.legal_issue: A reversioner who succeeds in recovering property alienated by a Hindu widow may receive mesne profits from the widow’s death, including where possession is conditional on repayment of an amount benefiting the estate if interest on that amount is allowed.
material_facts: The widow had transferred inherited property to transferees, and the ultimate reversioners sued for possession after her death.

The Court upheld recovery of some property because the relevant alienation was not binding on the reversioners; other property was recoverable subject to repayment of an amount found to have benefited the estate.
The conditional decree also required payment of interest on the amount to be repaid.
The High Court awarded mesne profits from the widow’s death and directed that their amount be determined separately.
issues.conclusion: The reversioners could be awarded mesne profits from the widow’s death; the conditional repayment of an estate-benefit amount did not prevent that award where interest was payable on the amount.
issues.legal_principle: A widow’s alienation is not automatically void, but it is voidable at the election of the reversioner, who may sue for possession without first obtaining a decree setting aside the alienation. Under the principle explained in Bijoya Gopal v. Krishna Mahishi, a successful possession claim is treated as establishing the transferee’s possession as unlawful from the widow’s death; the Court therefore allowed mesne profits for that period, consistent with Bhagwat Dayal v. Debi Dayal and Satgur Prasad v. Harinarain Singh. Banwarilal v. Mahesh was distinguished because it concerned a son’s claim against an alienee of a Mitakshara father. A conditional repayment order does not preclude mesne profits where interest is allowed on the repayment amount; the amount of mesne profits may be determined under Order XX, rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

rule.if: reversioner_possession_suit and widow_transferred_inherited_property and widow_alienation_not_binding_on_reversioner and reversioner_succeeded_in_claiming_possession and (not estate_benefit_repayment_required or interest_on_repayment_allowed)

predicates.reversioner_possession_suit: A claimant who asserts a right as the ultimate successor brings a suit to recover property from transferees.
predicates.widow_transferred_inherited_property: A widow transferred property that she held as an inherited estate.
predicates.widow_alienation_not_binding_on_reversio: The widow’s transfer was found not to bind the ultimate successor.
predicates.reversioner_succeeded_in_claiming_posses: The ultimate successor succeeded in obtaining a decree for possession of the property.
predicates.estate_benefit_repayment_required: The possession decree required the successor to repay an amount found to have benefited the estate.
predicates.interest_on_repayment_allowed: The decree allowed the transferee interest on the amount the successor was required to repay.

issues.definition: A successor who sues for possession and succeeds against a widow’s transferee is entitled to mesne profits where the transfer does not bind the successor; a repayment condition for an estate benefit does not prevent that entitlement if interest is allowed on the repayment.
